key_terms.term: On-state voltage of a diode (v<sub>D</sub> = V<sub>TO</sub> + i<sub>D</sub> r<sub>d</sub>)
key_terms.meaning: Threshold V<sub>TO</sub> (about 0.7 V to 0.8 V for silicon) plus the slope-resistance drop; about 1 V to 1.5 V at rated current
Time from the instant diode current crosses zero going negative until it falls back to a small specified value
Area of the negative current pulse at turn-off; Q<sub>rr</sub> ≈ ½ I<sub>RRM</sub> t<sub>rr</sub>; recovery loss P<sub>rr</sub> ≈ Q<sub>rr</sub> V<sub>s</sub> f<sub>s</sub>
Minimum anode current that keeps an SCR on when the gate pulse is removed; I<sub>L</sub> is larger than I<sub>H</sub>
Minimum anode current below which a conducting SCR turns off
PNPN thyristor drawn as a PNP and an NPN transistor whose collectors feed each other's bases; regeneration starts when α₁ + α₂ → 1
Anode-to-cathode voltage with the gate open at which the SCR turns on by junction avalanche

key_terms.term: Gate trigger current and voltage (I<sub>GT</sub>, V<sub>GT</sub>)
key_terms.meaning: Gate current and voltage sure to turn on every device of the type at a stated temperature; the drive must supply at least these
Gate pulse with a fast rise (well under 1 µs) and high initial current, so the SCR turns on quickly over the whole cathode area
A fast rising anode voltage pushes charging current C<sub>j</sub>·dv/dt through the junction capacitance, which acts like gate current and can turn the SCR on by mistake
T ≈ R C ln(1/(1 − η)), with peak-point voltage V<sub>P</sub> = η V<sub>BB</sub> + V<sub>D</sub>
Process of bringing anode current below holding current and holding reverse voltage long enough for the SCR to regain forward blocking
Time for which the circuit holds the SCR reverse-biased after current zero; t<sub>c</sub> = C V / I for capacitor commutation at constant current; t<sub>c</sub> must exceed t<sub>q</sub>
Turning off an SCR in a DC circuit by an external LC network, an auxiliary SCR or a transistor that forces current to zero
Two SCRs connected in inverse parallel on one chip with one gate; conducts and is triggered in both half cycles of AC
Two-terminal, bidirectional trigger diode that breaks over at about ±30 V and is used to fire a TRIAC
Thyristor turned off by a large negative gate current; turn-off gain β<sub>off</sub> = I<sub>A</sub> / I<sub>G(off)</sub>, only about 3 to 5
Flat part of v<sub>GS</sub> during switching while C<sub>gd</sub> is charged; the drain voltage swings in t<sub>fv</sub> = Q<sub>gd</sub> / I<sub>g</sub>
R-C across a device to limit dv/dt (C<sub>s</sub> = I / (dv/dt), loss ½ C<sub>s</sub> V² f<sub>s</sub> in R<sub>s</sub>), or a series L to limit di/dt (L<sub>s</sub> = V / (di/dt))
Loss from voltage-current overlap at each transition; P<sub>sw</sub> = ½ V I (t<sub>on</sub> + t<sub>off</sub>) f<sub>s</sub> with an inductive load (a sixth instead of a half with a resistive load)
Temperature rise per watt (°C/W); T<sub>j</sub> = T<sub>a</sub> + P (Rθ<sub>JC</sub> + Rθ<sub>CS</sub> + Rθ<sub>SA</sub>)
Material number ε μ E<sub>c</sub>³ that ranks a semiconductor for power devices; SiC and GaN beat silicon by hundreds of times

takeaways: A power diode is a switch with a fixed forward drop and a turn-off delay set by reverse recovery, so it matters most at high frequency.
An SCR is a four-layer latch: gate current only starts the regeneration, after which the anode current itself keeps the device on.
A gate trigger circuit must give a fast-rising pulse with enough current, lasting until the anode current passes the latching current, and inside the gate power limits.
Commutation is the circuit's job, not the device's: you must drop current below I<sub>H</sub> and then hold reverse voltage for longer than t<sub>q</sub>.
TRIAC and DIAC make a cheap, phase-controlled AC switch, while GTO gives a thyristor-like device that can be turned off from the gate.
Power BJT is current driven, MOSFET is voltage driven with a gate charge, and IGBT puts a MOSFET gate on a BJT output for high-voltage work.
Ratings mean nothing without protection: snubbers limit dv/dt and di/dt, and gate drives must deliver clean, fast pulses with isolated returns.
Switching loss and thermal resistance together decide the heat sink and the maximum switching frequency a design can survive.

SiC and GaN block the same voltage with a much thinner drift layer than silicon, so they conduct and switch with far less loss, but they demand tighter gate drive, careful layout and attention to interference.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the V–I characteristics and the two-transistor model with a neat sketch, the turn-on methods and commutation classes, and numerical work on switching loss, snubbers and heat sinks. Long answers are judged on correct sketches, numbers with units and protection reasoning that follows from the device characteristics.

bank.q: Draw and explain the static V–I characteristic of a power diode. Mark the threshold voltage, the on-state slope, the leakage region and the reverse breakdown voltage, and give typical values for a silicon power diode. Explain why a power diode has a lightly doped drift region.
outline: p<sup>+</sup> n<sup>−</sup> n<sup>+</sup> structure and the role of the drift region
Forward branch: threshold V<sub>TO</sub>, then a straight line of slope 1/r<sub>d</sub>; v<sub>D</sub> = V<sub>TO</sub> + i<sub>D</sub> r<sub>d</sub>
Reverse branch: leakage I<sub>R</sub> up to V<sub>RRM</sub>, breakdown at V<sub>BR</sub>
Typical values and the conduction-loss formula
answer: Structure. A power diode is a p<sup>+</sup> anode, a lightly doped n<sup>−</sup> drift region and an n<sup>+</sup> cathode. Current i<sub>D</sub> flows from anode A to cathode K and v<sub>D</sub> is measured from A to K.

answer: Forward region. Below the threshold (cut-in) voltage V<sub>TO</sub>, about 0.7 V to 0.8 V for silicon, almost no current flows. Above it the drift region is flooded with holes and electrons (conductivity modulation) and the curve is close to a straight line of slope 1/r<sub>d</sub>. Model: v<sub>D</sub> = V<sub>TO</sub> + i<sub>D</sub> r<sub>d</sub>. At rated current the drop is typically 1 V to 1.5 V; for example V<sub>TO</sub> = 0.85 V and r<sub>d</sub> = 12 mΩ give 0.97 V at 10 A.

Reverse region. With the cathode positive only a small leakage current I<sub>R</sub> flows, microamperes to milliamperes in a power diode, rising with temperature. The datasheet value V<sub>RRM</sub> is the repetitive peak reverse voltage that may be applied every cycle. At the breakdown voltage V<sub>BR</sub> the current rises sharply (avalanche); a power diode is never operated there.

Why the drift region is lightly doped. The reverse voltage is held by the depletion layer, and a lightly doped layer lets the depletion region spread wide, so a high V<sub>BR</sub> is reached without the field passing the critical value. A thicker drift region therefore means a higher voltage rating but a higher r<sub>d</sub> and on-state drop; conductivity modulation keeps the drop to about a volt in spite of the thick layer.

Losses from the characteristic. Conduction loss is P = V<sub>TO</sub> I<sub>avg</sub> + r<sub>d</sub> I<sub>rms</sub>². Example: I<sub>avg</sub> = 5 A, I<sub>rms</sub>² = 50 A², V<sub>TO</sub> = 0.85 V, r<sub>d</sub> = 12 mΩ give P = 4.25 + 0.60 = 4.85 W.

Ideal versus real. An ideal diode would have zero drop forward and zero current reverse; the real one has V<sub>TO</sub> and r<sub>d</sub> forward and I<sub>R</sub> reverse, and in switching it adds reverse recovery (not shown on the static curve, which is measured slowly).
Check: the model gives 0.85 + 10 × 0.012 = 0.97 V at 10 A and 0.85 + 30 × 0.012 = 1.21 V at 30 A, so if 30 A is the rated current the drop falls inside the 1 V to 1.5 V band quoted above.

bank.q: Explain the two-transistor model of an SCR and use it to derive the anode current. Show why the device latches on and why the gate cannot turn it off.
outline: Split P1 N1 P2 N2 into p-n-p T1 and n-p-n T2 with a sketch
I<sub>C1</sub> = α₁I<sub>A</sub> + I<sub>CBO1</sub>, I<sub>C2</sub> = α₂I<sub>K</sub> + I<sub>CBO2</sub>, I<sub>K</sub> = I<sub>A</sub> + I<sub>G</sub>
I<sub>A</sub> = (α₂I<sub>G</sub> + I<sub>CBO1</sub> + I<sub>CBO2</sub>)/(1 − (α₁ + α₂))
α rises with current, so α₁ + α₂ → 1 and the loop latches; gate loses control
answer: Splitting the layers. Cut the P1-N1-P2-N2 structure along the middle layers. P1-N1-P2 forms a p-n-p transistor T1 whose emitter is the anode; N1-P2-N2 forms an n-p-n transistor T2 whose emitter is the cathode and whose base is the gate layer. N1 is both the base of T1 and the collector of T2; P2 is both the collector of T1 and the base of T2.

answer.text: Currents. With common-base gains α₁, α₂ and leakage currents I<sub>CBO1</sub>, I<sub>CBO2</sub>:
answer.pre:
I<sub>C1</sub> = α₁ I<sub>A</sub> + I<sub>CBO1</sub>
I<sub>C2</sub> = α₂ I<sub>K</sub> + I<sub>CBO2</sub>
I<sub>K</sub>  = I<sub>A</sub> + I<sub>G</sub>          (current entering = current leaving)
I<sub>A</sub>  = I<sub>C1</sub> + I<sub>C2</sub>         (current into the N1 node)

I<sub>A</sub> = α₁ I<sub>A</sub> + I<sub>CBO1</sub> + α₂ (I<sub>A</sub> + I<sub>G</sub>) + I<sub>CBO2</sub>
I<sub>A</sub> (1 − α₁ − α₂) = α₂ I<sub>G</sub> + I<sub>CBO1</sub> + I<sub>CBO2</sub>
I<sub>A</sub> = (α₂ I<sub>G</sub> + I<sub>CBO1</sub> + I<sub>CBO2</sub>) / (1 − (α₁ + α₂))

answer: Blocking. At small currents silicon transistors have small α, so α₁ + α₂ is well below 1 and I<sub>A</sub> is only a little larger than the leakage terms: the SCR is in forward blocking.

answer.text: Turn-on by the gate, with numbers. Take I<sub>G</sub> = 20 mA and I<sub>CBO1</sub> + I<sub>CBO2</sub> = 10 µA:

head: α₁
α₂
1 − (α₁ + α₂)
I<sub>A</sub>
rows: set by the load, e.g. 200 V ÷ 20 Ω = 10 A

answer: Regeneration. Gate current raises the current in T2; its collector current is base current for T1, whose collector current is more base current for T2. As the currents grow, α₁ and α₂ grow, the denominator falls towards zero and the anode current runs away until only the external circuit limits it. At α₁ + α₂ = 1 the loop gain is one: the SCR has latched.

Why the gate loses control. Once latched, each transistor supplies the other's base current, so I<sub>G</sub> is no longer needed; removing it leaves α₁ + α₂ ≥ 1 and conduction continues. A reverse gate current in an ordinary SCR is far too small to pull the n-p-n out of saturation over the whole cathode (the GTO's interdigitated gate does that with a current of a quarter or so of the anode current). Turn-off needs the anode current below I<sub>H</sub> by the circuit.

Other turn-on methods in the same model: a high anode voltage (breakover), dv/dt, heat or light each raise the leakage terms or the currents, drive α₁ + α₂ to 1 and latch the device without a gate pulse.

Check: with the second set of gains the numerator 0.5 × 0.020 + 0.000 01 = 0.010 01 A and 0.010 01 ÷ 0.02 = 0.5005 A; the same 20 mA gate current gives about 8 times the current of the first set, which shows the runaway.

bank.q: List the methods of turning on a thyristor and explain each with a short note. Which methods are used deliberately and which must be prevented?
outline: Gate, forward voltage, dv/dt, temperature, light
Mechanism of each in terms of J2 and regeneration
Gate and light are deliberate; the rest are prevented, and how
Gate pulse requirements
answer: Starting point. An SCR in forward blocking has J1 and J3 forward biased and J2 reverse biased. Any action that drives enough carriers across J2 to make α₁ + α₂ reach 1 turns it on. There are five.

Gate triggering. A positive gate-cathode current injects electrons from the cathode into P2; regeneration starts and the SCR latches once the anode current passes I<sub>L</sub>. The gate source must supply at least I<sub>GT</sub> at V<sub>GT</sub> (for example 100 mA at 1.5 V) and stay inside the gate power limits. This is the normal, controlled method, used in rectifiers, choppers and AC controllers.

Forward-voltage (breakover) triggering. With I<sub>G</sub> = 0, raising V<sub>AK</sub> to V<sub>BO</sub> makes J2 break down by avalanche; the large current then latches the device. It is not used for control because the current concentrates in a small area and can damage the SCR. It is prevented by derating: the working voltage is kept at 60 % to 70 % of V<sub>DRM</sub>.

dv/dt triggering. J2 behaves like a capacitor C<sub>j</sub>. A fast rise of anode voltage drives a charging current i = C<sub>j</sub> dv/dt through it, which acts like gate current; above the rated critical dv/dt the SCR turns on falsely. Prevented by an R-C snubber across the SCR, which slows the voltage rise (dv/dt = I/C<sub>s</sub> at turn-off).

Temperature triggering. Leakage current across J2 rises steeply with junction temperature; at a high temperature the leakage alone can start regeneration. Prevented by keeping the junction below T<sub>j(max)</sub> with a proper heat sink, T<sub>j</sub> = T<sub>a</sub> + P ΣRθ.

Light triggering. Photons falling on the gate region create electron-hole pairs at J2. A light-activated SCR (LASCR) is fired deliberately by a light pulse through an optical fibre, which isolates the control from the high voltage; it is used in HVDC valves.

Good gate pulse. Fast rise (well under 1 µs), initial current several times I<sub>GT</sub>, and width long enough for the anode current to pass I<sub>L</sub>; for example a 100 V, 20 Ω, 0.5 H load with I<sub>L</sub> = 50 mA needs about 251 µs.

bank.q: Compare TRIAC, DIAC and GTO with respect to structure, terminals, V–I characteristic, triggering and turn-off, and typical applications.
outline: TRIAC: two SCRs in inverse parallel, MT1 MT2 G, four triggering modes
DIAC: two terminals, symmetric breakover about ±30 V, trigger only
GTO: interdigitated gate, negative gate turn-off, β<sub>off</sub> 3 to 5
Applications and a comparison table
answer: TRIAC. A five-layer device that acts like two SCRs in inverse parallel with one gate. Terminals MT1, MT2 and gate G (near MT1); polarities are measured from MT1. Its V–I curve has identical blocking and conduction branches in the first and third quadrants. It is triggered in four modes (I+, I−, III−, III+); I+ is the most sensitive and III+ the least, so I+ and III− are preferred. It turns off at the current zero like an SCR, and with inductive loads it needs a snubber against commutating dv/dt.

DIAC. A two-terminal bidirectional trigger diode with no gate. It blocks in both directions until about ±30 V (V<sub>BO</sub>), then its voltage drops by several volts (negative resistance) and it passes a current pulse. It carries no load current: it fires a TRIAC from an R-C phase-shift network so that the firing angle is the same in both half-cycles.

answer.text: GTO. A p-n-p-n thyristor with the cathode split into fingers surrounded by gate metal and a low-gain p-n-p section. A positive gate pulse turns it on; a negative gate current of I<sub>A</sub>/β<sub>off</sub> turns it off. Example with β<sub>off</sub> = 4:
answer.pre:
I<sub>G(off)</sub> = I<sub>A</sub> / β<sub>off</sub> = 600 A / 4 = 150 A
Gate charge (triangle, 20 µs) = ½ × 150 × 20 µs = 1.5 mC
Energy from a 15 V gate supply = 15 × 1.5 mC = 22.5 mJ per turn-off
At 500 Hz: 22.5 mJ × 500 = 11.25 W of gate supply power

head: Feature
TRIAC
DIAC
GTO
rows: up to a few tens of A at 50 Hz

answer: Dimmer numbers. A TRIAC dimmer firing at 90° on 230 V into 100 Ω gives V<sub>rms</sub> = 230 × √0.5 = 162.6 V and P = 264.5 W, half the 529 W at full conduction.

Conclusion. The TRIAC is the cheap AC switch, the DIAC is only its trigger, and the GTO is the high-power DC switch that needs no commutation circuit but a strong negative gate drive (150 A for 600 A in the example).

bank.q: An SCR has V<sub>GT</sub> = 1.0 V, I<sub>GT</sub> = 100 mA and a latching current of 40 mA. It feeds R = 40 Ω in series with L = 0.4 H from a 200 V DC supply, and is fired from a 12 V source through a 1:1 pulse transformer. Draw the trigger arrangement, find the series gate resistor and its peak power, the minimum width of a single gate pulse, and the average gate-resistor power if the chosen pulse repeats at 50 Hz.
outline: Pulse transformer isolates the 12 V control side; series R, gate-cathode resistor, diode for reverse pulse
R<sub>s</sub> = (V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>GT</sub>)/I<sub>GT</sub>; peak power I²R
i(t) = (V/R)(1 − e<sup>−Rt/L</sup>); pulse lasts until i = I<sub>L</sub>
Average power = peak × duty; transformer volt-seconds
answer: Arrangement. The control transistor switches 12 V across the primary of a 1:1 pulse transformer. The secondary drives the gate through the series resistor R<sub>s</sub>; a diode in series blocks the negative swing when the core resets, and a small resistor (a few hundred ohms) from gate to cathode keeps the gate quiet against noise. The transformer isolates the 12 V control circuit from the 200 V power circuit.

answer.pre:
Voltage across R<sub>s</sub> = 12 − 1.0 = 11 V
R<sub>s</sub> = 11 V / 0.100 A = 110 Ω
Peak power in R<sub>s</sub> = I<sub>GT</sub>² R<sub>s</sub> = 0.1² × 110 = 1.1 W
Peak gate power = V<sub>GT</sub> I<sub>GT</sub> = 1.0 × 0.1 = 0.1 W

answer.text: Minimum pulse width. After turn-on the anode current rises with the load time constant:

answer: Choice. A 100 µs pulse gives a margin of 100 ÷ 80.3 = 1.25; check i(100 µs) = 5 × (1 − e<sup>−0.01</sup>) = 5 × 0.00995 = 49.8 mA, above I<sub>L</sub> = 40 mA.

answer.text: Average powers at one pulse per 20 ms (50 Hz):
answer.pre:
Duty = 100 µs / 20 ms = 0.005
Average power in R<sub>s</sub> = 1.1 W × 0.005 = 5.5 mW
Average gate power   = 0.1 W × 0.005 = 0.5 mW

answer: Pulse transformer. The core must carry 12 V for 100 µs, a volt-second product of 12 × 100 × 10<sup>−6</sup> = 1.2 mV·s, without saturating; a longer pulse would need a bigger core, which is why long gate signals are sent as pulse trains.
Check: with a 10 µs pulse the current would reach only 5 × (1 − e<sup>−0.001</sup>) = 5.0 mA, far below 40 mA, so the SCR would turn off when the pulse ends. The 100 µs pulse is necessary.

bank.q: Explain natural and forced commutation. For an impulse (auxiliary) commutated chopper, show how the circuit turn-off time t<sub>c</sub> is found and state the design condition on t<sub>q</sub>. Design the commutating capacitor for a 150 V supply, a 30 A load and an SCR with t<sub>q</sub> = 40 µs, using a safety factor of 1.5.
outline: Natural (line) commutation: AC supply reverses, current zero, class F
Forced commutation: DC supply, capacitor reverse-biases the SCR, classes A to E
t<sub>c</sub> = C V / I for constant load current; t<sub>c</sub> > t<sub>q</sub> with margin
Design and check of C
answer: Why commutation is needed. A latched SCR stays on while its anode current exceeds I<sub>H</sub>. To turn it off the current must be brought below I<sub>H</sub> and the SCR held reverse-biased until its stored charge has recombined, a time t<sub>q</sub> given on the datasheet.

Natural commutation. With an AC supply the anode voltage reverses each half-cycle, the current falls to zero and the SCR is reverse-biased for the rest of the half-cycle. No extra components are needed; it is used in controlled rectifiers, AC voltage controllers and cycloconverters (class F).

Forced commutation. With a DC supply the current never falls by itself, so a pre-charged capacitor (or a resonant L-C circuit) is switched across the conducting SCR to reverse-bias it and take its current. Classes A (load), B (resonant pulse), C (complementary), D (impulse or auxiliary) and E (external pulse) are forced methods.

Impulse commutation. The capacitor C, charged to V with the polarity that reverse-biases the main SCR, is connected across it by firing the auxiliary SCR. The load current I (held constant by the load inductance) now flows through the capacitor, the main SCR's current falls to zero, and its voltage equals the capacitor voltage.

answer.pre:
Capacitor discharges at constant current:  dv/dt = I / C
SCR voltage goes from −V to 0 in  t<sub>c</sub> = C V / I
Condition:  t<sub>c</sub> > t<sub>q</sub>  (with a safety factor k: t<sub>c</sub> = k t<sub>q</sub>)
Design rule:  C ≥ I k t<sub>q</sub> / V

Required t<sub>c</sub> = 1.5 × 40 µs = 60 µs
C = I t<sub>c</sub> / V = 30 × 60 × 10⁻⁶ / 150 = 12 × 10⁻⁶ F = 12 µF
Capacitor voltage rating above 150 V (choose 250 V or more)

answer: Check: t<sub>c</sub> = 12 × 10<sup>−6</sup> × 150 ÷ 30 = 60 µs = 1.5 × 40 µs. If the load current rose to 45 A, t<sub>c</sub> would fall to 40 µs, exactly t<sub>q</sub> and with no margin, so the capacitor must be sized for the largest load current.

Contrast with class C. With resistive loads the reverse voltage of the outgoing SCR swings through its load resistor R1, so t<sub>c</sub> = 0.693 R1 C instead; C V / I applies only when the current stays constant during commutation.

bank.q: A power MOSFET switches 300 V and 5 A at 100 kHz with an inductive load. Its turn-on and turn-off transition times are 80 ns and 120 ns, its on-state resistance is 0.5 Ω and the duty ratio is 0.5. Estimate the switching loss and the conduction loss, compare them, and find the total loss at 50 kHz.
outline: P<sub>sw</sub> = ½ V I (t<sub>on</sub> + t<sub>off</sub>) f<sub>s</sub> for an inductive load
P<sub>cond</sub> = I² R<sub>DS(on)</sub> D
Compare and total; frequency dependence
Resistive-load factor 1/6 for comparison
answer: Model. With a clamped inductive load each transition is a triangle of power of peak V I, so each transition costs ½ V I t, and a cycle has one turn-on and one turn-off.

answer.pre: P<sub>cond</sub> = I² R<sub>DS(on)</sub> D = 5² × 0.5 × 0.5 = 6.25 W

answer: Comparison. Total P = 15 + 6.25 = 21.25 W, and switching is 15 ÷ 21.25 = 70.6 % of it. At this frequency the switching loss dominates; a faster gate drive (shorter transitions) helps more than a lower R<sub>DS(on)</sub>.

Why only P<sub>sw</sub> halves. Switching energy per cycle is fixed (150 µJ), so P<sub>sw</sub> is proportional to f<sub>s</sub>; conduction loss depends on the current, R<sub>DS(on)</sub> and the duty ratio, not on frequency.

Resistive-load comparison. If the load were resistive, voltage and current would change together and each transition would cost V I t/6: P<sub>sw</sub> = 300 × 5 × 200 × 10<sup>−9</sup> ÷ 6 × 100 000 = 5 W, a third of the inductive value. Using the resistive formula here would under-estimate the loss.

answer.text: Frequency at which the two losses are equal:
answer.pre:
P<sub>sw</sub> = P<sub>cond</sub>  →  150 µJ × f<sub>s</sub> = 6.25 W  →  f<sub>s</sub> = 6.25 / 150 × 10⁻⁶ = 41.7 kHz
Below about 42 kHz conduction loss dominates; above it switching loss dominates.

answer: Reducing the loss. A stronger gate drive that halves both transition times (40 ns and 60 ns) halves P<sub>sw</sub> to 7.5 W at 100 kHz, so the total falls from 21.25 W to 13.75 W; a MOSFET with half the R<sub>DS(on)</sub> would save only 3.1 W. Soft switching, which makes either the voltage or the current zero during the transition, removes most of P<sub>sw</sub> and is the reason resonant converters can run at hundreds of kilohertz.

answer.text: Thermal check (taking, as an example, a total junction-to-ambient resistance of 3 °C/W and 40 °C air):

answer: Check: E per transition at turn-off = ½ × 300 × 5 × 120 ns = 90 µJ and at turn-on 60 µJ, summing to 150 µJ as used.

bank.q: Design a turn-off R-C snubber for a device that switches 400 V and 10 A at 5 kHz, with a rated dv/dt of 200 V/µs and a stray loop inductance of 0.2 µH. Choose C and R, find the resistor's power, check the discharge time and justify the component ratings.
outline: C<sub>s</sub> = I/(dv/dt)
R<sub>s</sub> between the damping value 2√(L/C) and the discharge-current limit V/R
Energy ½ C V², power ½ C V² f<sub>s</sub>, resistor rating
Discharge time 3 R C against the minimum on-time
answer: Purpose. At turn-off the snubber capacitor takes the load current, so the device voltage rises at I/C<sub>s</sub> instead of almost instantly; the switching overlap and the dv/dt stress fall, and the energy goes to R<sub>s</sub> at the next turn-on.

answer.pre:
dv/dt = I / C<sub>s</sub>  →  C<sub>s</sub> = 10 A / (200 × 10⁶ V/s) = 50 × 10⁻⁹ F = 50 nF
Voltage rating: above 400 V plus overshoot (choose 630 V or 1 kV, pulse-rated film)

answer.text: Resistor, lower limit from damping the stray inductance with C<sub>s</sub>:
answer.pre:
Series L-C-R ringing: ζ = (R/2)√(C/L); for ζ = 1:
R = 2√(L/C) = 2 × √(0.2 × 10⁻⁶ / 50 × 10⁻⁹) = 2 × √4 = 4 Ω
Ringing frequency without damping: 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1.59 MHz

answer: Resistor, upper side from the discharge current. At turn-on C<sub>s</sub> discharges through R<sub>s</sub> and the device with peak current 400/R<sub>s</sub>. Limiting it to 4 A (a modest addition to the 10 A load current) gives R<sub>s</sub> = 400 ÷ 4 = 100 Ω, well above the 4 Ω damping limit, so the ringing is also damped. Choose R<sub>s</sub> = 100 Ω.

answer.pre:
E = ½ C<sub>s</sub> V² = 0.5 × 50 × 10⁻⁹ × 400² = 4 × 10⁻³ J = 4 mJ
P<sub>Rs</sub> = E f<sub>s</sub> = 4 mJ × 5000 = 20 W

answer: Resistor rating. The resistor carries 20 W on average and a 4 A peak; choose a non-inductive (thick-film or carbon-composition) resistor of 25 W to 30 W on a heat sink. A wire-wound resistor's inductance would spoil the snubber.

answer.pre:
3 R<sub>s</sub> C<sub>s</sub> = 3 × 100 × 50 × 10⁻⁹ = 15 µs
At 5 kHz the period is 200 µs, so the device must stay on at least 15 µs (D ≥ 0.075)

answer: Diode option. A fast diode across R<sub>s</sub> (polarised snubber) lets C<sub>s</sub> charge directly at turn-off, so the dv/dt limit is met exactly, while the discharge still goes through R<sub>s</sub>.

Check: with C<sub>s</sub> = 50 nF the voltage takes 400 ÷ 200 V/µs = 2 µs to rise at turn-off, and I × 2 µs = 10 × 2 × 10<sup>−6</sup> = 20 µC = C<sub>s</sub> V = 50 nF × 400 V, so the design is consistent.

bank.q: A MOSFET has gate charge Q<sub>g</sub> = 60 nC, Q<sub>gd</sub> = 20 nC and a plateau voltage of 5 V. It is driven between 0 and 10 V at 100 kHz. Calculate the gate drive power and the average driver current, and explain with numbers why a gate resistor of 10 Ω gives slower switching than 2 Ω.
outline: P<sub>gate</sub> = Q<sub>g</sub> V<sub>drive</sub> f<sub>s</sub>, independent of R<sub>g</sub>
Average current Q<sub>g</sub> f<sub>s</sub>
Plateau current (V<sub>drive</sub> − V<sub>pl</sub>)/R<sub>g</sub> and t<sub>fv</sub> = Q<sub>gd</sub>/I<sub>g</sub> for both resistors
Trade-off: speed and loss against dv/dt and interference

answer.pre:
P<sub>gate</sub> = Q<sub>g</sub> V<sub>drive</sub> f<sub>s</sub> = 60 × 10⁻⁹ × 10 × 100 000 = 0.06 W = 60 mW
Average driver current = Q<sub>g</sub> f<sub>s</sub> = 60 × 10⁻⁹ × 100 000 = 6 mA

answer: Where the power goes. Each cycle the driver puts Q<sub>g</sub> V<sub>drive</sub> = 0.6 µJ into the gate and takes it out again; it is dissipated in the gate resistor, the driver and the MOSFET's internal gate resistance. The total does not depend on R<sub>g</sub>, only on how it is shared.

answer.text: Switching speed on the Miller plateau:

answer: Explanation. On the plateau the gate voltage is fixed at 5 V, so the gate current is set by (V<sub>drive</sub> − V<sub>pl</sub>)/R<sub>g</sub>. The drain voltage can only change as fast as this current moves the Q<sub>gd</sub> charge, so a five times larger resistor makes the voltage edge five times slower: 40 ns instead of 8 ns.

Effect on loss. With, for example, 200 V and 10 A switched, the voltage-fall loss per edge is ½ V I t<sub>fv</sub>: 0.5 × 200 × 10 × 40 ns = 40 µJ with 10 Ω against 8 µJ with 2 Ω; at 100 kHz that is 4 W against 0.8 W for this interval alone.

The price of a small R<sub>g</sub>. The 2 Ω drive gives dv/dt = 200 V ÷ 8 ns = 25 V/ns, against 5 V/ns with 10 Ω, so more ringing, more interference and more Miller current into the other switch of a bridge, and the driver must deliver 5 A peaks. The chosen R<sub>g</sub> is a compromise, checked on the bench.

Practical choice. Many drivers use separate turn-on and turn-off resistors (a diode steers the current): for example 10 Ω for turn-on to limit dv/dt and the diode recovery current, and 2 Ω for turn-off so that the gate is held firmly low against Miller current.
Check: average current × drive voltage = 6 mA × 10 V = 60 mW, the same as Q<sub>g</sub> V<sub>drive</sub> f<sub>s</sub>, and it does not change with R<sub>g</sub>; only the speed does.

bank.q: Compare power BJT, power MOSFET and IGBT on drive, conduction drop, switching speed, second breakdown and safe operating area, and say which you would pick for a 400 V, 20 kHz, 20 A motor drive. Use the illustrative datasheet values V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> = 1.8 V for a 600 V IGBT and R<sub>DS(on)</sub> = 0.15 Ω (hot) for a 600 V silicon MOSFET.
outline: Structure and drive of each device
Conduction drop, switching speed, SOA and second breakdown
Comparison table
Numbers at 20 A and the choice with reasons
answer: Power BJT. Vertical n-p-n, driven by base current; β is only 5 to 20, so a 20 A switch needs 1 A to 4 A of continuous base current and a strong driver. V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> is 1 V to 2 V. Stored charge in the base and drift region makes turn-off slow (microseconds), so it is limited to a few kHz to about 20 kHz. Current crowding causes second breakdown, so its forward-bias and reverse-bias SOA are restricted.

Power MOSFET. Majority-carrier device driven by gate voltage; the gate needs only Q<sub>g</sub> at each edge, so the drive is simple. It switches in tens of nanoseconds, so it suits 50 kHz to MHz. On, it is a resistance R<sub>DS(on)</sub> with a positive temperature coefficient, so it shares current in parallel and has no second breakdown; its SOA is limited only thermally. R<sub>DS(on)</sub> rises steeply with voltage rating, so at 600 V the conduction loss is high.

IGBT. MOSFET gate with a bipolar output: easy voltage drive, and conductivity modulation gives a low V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> of 1.5 V to 2.5 V even at 600 V to 6.5 kV. The tail current at turn-off limits it to about 20 kHz to 50 kHz. It has a wide, square SOA, but its parasitic thyristor must not latch up; most need an inverse diode.

answer.text: Conduction loss at 20 A (switch conducting half the time, D = 0.5):
answer.pre:
IGBT:    1.8 V × 20 A × 0.5 = 18 W
MOSFET:  20² × 0.15 × 0.5  = 30 W
Crossover current = V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> / R<sub>DS(on)</sub> = 1.8 / 0.15 = 12 A

answer: Voltage. On a 400 V link, overshoot at turn-off and derating (working voltage about 60 % to 70 % of rating) call for 600 V or 650 V devices. 400 V is 67 % of 600 V, at the limit of the usual derating.
Frequency. 20 kHz is just above hearing, which is why motor drives use it; it is inside the IGBT's range, too fast for a BJT, and easy for a MOSFET.

Choice. Pick the 600 V IGBT (with its inverse diode, often in a six-pack module). At 20 A its conduction loss is 18 W against 30 W for the MOSFET, since 20 A is above the 12 A crossover, its switching loss at 20 kHz is acceptable, and its drive is as simple as a MOSFET's. The BJT is rejected for its drive power, its slowness and second breakdown. A 650 V SiC MOSFET would cut switching loss further at a higher cost.

Check: if the drive ran at 5 A instead, the MOSFET would lose 5² × 0.15 × 0.5 = 1.9 W against 1.8 × 5 × 0.5 = 4.5 W for the IGBT; below the 12 A crossover the MOSFET wins, so the choice depends on the current.

bank.q: A thyristor in a DC chopper has t<sub>q</sub> = 30 µs, but its impulse commutation circuit (C = 5 µF, charged to 100 V) holds reverse voltage for only 25 µs at full load. Analyse what happens, find the full-load current, and discuss with numbers three ways to fix the circuit.
outline: t<sub>c</sub> < t<sub>q</sub>: the SCR re-fires when forward voltage returns
Load current from t<sub>c</sub> = C V / I
Fixes: larger C, lower current, faster SCR, cooler junction
Consequences: loss of control, commutation failure, fuse blows
answer: What happens. At the end of the 25 µs the capacitor voltage reverses and forward voltage reappears across the SCR, whose stored charge has not yet recombined (it needs 30 µs). The SCR turns on again without a gate pulse. The chopper loses control: the load sees the full supply, the commutating capacitor charges the wrong way, and the next commutation attempt fails too. In practice the over-current trips the protection or blows the fuse.

answer.pre: t<sub>c</sub> = C V / I  →  I = C V / t<sub>c</sub> = 5 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 / 25 × 10⁻⁶ = 20 A

answer: Why it may work at light load. At lower current the capacitor discharges more slowly: at 10 A, t<sub>c</sub> = 5 × 10<sup>−6</sup> × 100 ÷ 10 = 50 µs > 30 µs, so the fault appears only near full load, and gets worse when the junction is hot because t<sub>q</sub> grows with temperature.

answer.pre:
Required t<sub>c</sub> = 1.5 × 30 = 45 µs
C = I t<sub>c</sub> / V = 20 × 45 × 10⁻⁶ / 100 = 9 × 10⁻⁶ F = 9 µF (choose 10 µF)
Check: t<sub>c</sub> = 10 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 / 20 = 50 µs

answer: Fix 2, a faster SCR. Keep C = 5 µF and choose an inverter-grade SCR with t<sub>q</sub> ≤ 25 ÷ 1.5 = 16.7 µs. Cost is higher but the commutation circuit is unchanged.

answer.pre: For t<sub>c</sub> = 45 µs with C = 5 µF:  I<sub>max</sub> = C V / t<sub>c</sub> = 5 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 / 45 × 10⁻⁶ = 11.1 A

answer: Other measures. Raising the capacitor voltage (for example with a resonant reversal that overcharges it) lengthens t<sub>c</sub> in proportion to V; better cooling keeps t<sub>q</sub> at its low-temperature value; and a current limit in the controller prevents operation above the safe current. A larger C, however, adds commutation loss and a longer commutation interval, which limits the minimum duty ratio.
Conclusion. The circuit is under-designed by a factor of 25 ÷ 30 = 0.83 at full load; the cheapest reliable fix is C = 10 µF, giving t<sub>c</sub> = 50 µs = 1.67 t<sub>q</sub>.

bank.q: Evaluate the claim that a silicon carbide MOSFET can replace a silicon IGBT in an 800 V, 50 kHz converter carrying 40 A. Suppose the 1200 V datasheets give, at 600 V and 40 A: IGBT V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> = 1.8 V and E<sub>on</sub> + E<sub>off</sub> = 5 mJ; SiC MOSFET R<sub>DS(on)</sub> = 40 mΩ (hot) and E<sub>on</sub> + E<sub>off</sub> = 1 mJ. Take the duty ratio as 0.5 and scale the energies in proportion to voltage. Discuss the benefits and the practical problems.
outline: Why SiC switches faster: unipolar, no tail, thin drift layer
Loss calculation for both at 800 V, 40 A, 50 kHz
Practical issues: gate drive, dv/dt and layout, short-circuit time, body diode, cost
Verdict
answer: Device physics. SiC's critical field (about 2.2 MV/cm against 0.3 MV/cm) lets a 1200 V drift layer be about 11 µm thick instead of about 80 µm for silicon, so a 1200 V SiC MOSFET has a low R<sub>DS(on)</sub>. It is unipolar: no stored charge and no tail current, so its switching energy is several times smaller than an IGBT's.

answer.pre:
IGBT:  5 mJ × 800/600 = 6.67 mJ per cycle
SiC:   1 mJ × 800/600 = 1.33 mJ per cycle

answer: Reading the numbers. The IGBT would have to remove 369 W from one die, which is beyond any practical heat sink, so a silicon IGBT cannot run this converter at 50 kHz; at 50 kHz it is the switching loss, not the conduction loss, that disqualifies it. The SiC MOSFET's 98.7 W is large but manageable with a good heat sink. The claim is therefore true at this frequency, and SiC also allows higher frequency, smaller inductors and filters, and a hotter junction.
Gate drive. SiC needs about +15 V to +20 V on and 0 V to −5 V off, with tight limits on the oxide; an IGBT driver at ±15 V must be changed. The negative bias also guards against Miller turn-on.

dv/dt and layout. Switching 800 V in about 20 ns is 40 V/ns. Through 50 pF of stray capacitance that drives 2 A of displacement current; the power loop and gate loop inductance must be small, and common-mode interference to the motor or the control circuit grows. Gate resistors and careful layout are needed, which give back part of the switching advantage.

Short circuits and body diode. A SiC MOSFET withstands a short circuit for only a few microseconds, less than a typical IGBT, so the driver's desaturation protection must act faster. Its body diode drops about 3 V, so dead times must be short or an external SiC Schottky diode added.

Cost and verdict. The SiC device and its driver cost more, but the system saves heat sink, magnetics and efficiency. Verdict: at 800 V and 50 kHz the replacement is justified and in fact necessary; the claim holds provided the gate drive, layout, protection and interference are redesigned, not just the device swapped.

Check: at 10 kHz the IGBT would lose 6.67 × 10 + 36 = 102.7 W against 13.3 + 32 = 45.3 W for SiC; at low frequency the IGBT becomes usable and the case for SiC rests on efficiency rather than feasibility.

bank.q: Two identical SCRs are connected in series to block 2 kV. Each is rated 1200 V; their off-state leakage currents may differ by 10 mA and their recovery charges by 20 µC. Explain the problem, design the static and dynamic sharing networks, find the string's derating factor and state how you would verify the sharing experimentally.
outline: Unequal leakage and recovery give unequal voltage sharing
Static resistor R ≤ (n V<sub>bm</sub> − V<sub>s</sub>)/((n − 1)ΔI<sub>b</sub>)
Dynamic capacitor C ≥ (n − 1)ΔQ/(n V<sub>bm</sub> − V<sub>s</sub>), with a series resistor
Derating factor and a test method
answer: The problem. Series SCRs carry the same leakage current when off, but their V–I curves differ, so the device with the lower leakage takes the larger share of the voltage. During turn-off the SCR that recovers first (smaller Q<sub>rr</sub>) must block the whole voltage alone until the others recover, and during turn-on the last to fire sees the whole voltage. Without sharing networks one SCR can exceed its 1200 V rating even though the string is rated 2400 V.

answer.text: Static sharing. A resistor R across each SCR carries a current much larger than the leakage difference. For n devices, the worst case has one device with the lowest leakage blocking V<sub>bm</sub>:
answer.pre:
R ≤ (n V<sub>bm</sub> − V<sub>s</sub>) / ((n − 1) ΔI<sub>b</sub>)
  = (2 × 1200 − 2000) / ((2 − 1) × 0.010)
  = 400 / 0.010 = 40 kΩ
Loss in each resistor at 1000 V: 1000² / 40 000 = 25 W  (choose about 35 kΩ, 30 W or more)

answer.text: Dynamic sharing. A capacitor across each SCR absorbs the difference in recovery charge:

answer: Series resistor and diode. Each capacitor has a small series resistor (tens of ohms) to limit its discharge current into the SCR at turn-on (di/dt), with a diode across the resistor so that the capacitor still acts at once at turn-off.

Firing. Both SCRs must be fired at the same instant with strong (hard) gate pulses from an isolated source, for example a pulse transformer with two secondaries, so that neither is left blocking the full voltage at turn-on.

Verification. With the gates off, apply the DC string voltage and measure each SCR's voltage with a high-voltage divider: each should be within the design limit (here no more than 1200 V; with matched leakage, about 1000 V each). Then run the circuit and record each SCR's voltage with differential probes through turn-on and turn-off: the transient peaks should stay below the 1200 V rating, and the two waveforms should cross over within microseconds.

Check: with R = 40 kΩ, a 10 mA leakage difference shifts the sharing by 0.010 × 40 000 ÷ 2 = 200 V from the 1000 V midpoint, so the worse device sees 1200 V, exactly its rating; a slightly smaller R gives margin.

bank.q: A converter fails in the field with short-circuited switches and signs of excessive junction temperature. Evaluate the roles of snubber design, gate drive and heat-sink selection in preventing such failures, using the device of the switching-loss worked example (40 W total loss, Rθ<sub>JC</sub> = 1.0 °C/W, Rθ<sub>CS</sub> = 0.5 °C/W, heat sink 0.6 °C/W, designed for 40 °C ambient, T<sub>j,max</sub> = 125 °C).
outline: Thermal check at design and at hot ambient or fan failure
Snubber: dv/dt false turn-on, overshoot, switching loss
Gate drive: Miller turn-on, negative bias, R<sub>g</sub>, desaturation protection
Combined failure chain and an evaluation of the fixes
answer: How the failures connect. A switch that runs hot has a higher leakage and longer turn-off, more switching loss, and a lower safe current; a switch that turns on falsely shorts the DC link (shoot-through) and fails as a short circuit. So heat, snubber and gate drive faults reinforce each other.

Evaluation of the heat sink. The design leaves only 1 °C of margin at 40 °C, so a hot cabinet or a dusty, slow fan pushes the junction past 125 °C. A sound design allows for the worst ambient and a derated fan: for 50 °C and T<sub>j</sub> ≤ 115 °C, ΣRθ ≤ 65 ÷ 40 = 1.625 °C/W, so Rθ<sub>SA</sub> ≤ 0.125 °C/W, which needs forced air or a lower-loss device. Heat-sink selection is the first line of defence.

Snubber. Without an adequate snubber, fast dv/dt at turn-off drives C dv/dt current into the device and the overshoot from stray inductance (v = L di/dt) can exceed the voltage rating; in thyristor circuits dv/dt causes false turn-on. A snubber with C<sub>s</sub> = I/(dv/dt) limits both and moves part of the turn-off loss into R<sub>s</sub>; but an oversized C<sub>s</sub> raises the R<sub>s</sub> loss (½ C<sub>s</sub> V² f<sub>s</sub>) and the turn-on current, so it must be sized, not just added.

Gate drive. If the off-state gate is held at 0 V through a weak path, the Miller current C<sub>gc</sub> dv/dt from the other switch's turn-on can lift it past threshold and both switches of a leg conduct. A −5 V to −8 V off bias, a low-impedance turn-off path or a Miller clamp prevents this; a dead time between the two gate signals is also needed. Too large an R<sub>g</sub> raises switching loss and temperature; too small an R<sub>g</sub> raises dv/dt and ringing. A driver with desaturation detection turns the device off softly within microseconds of a short circuit, before it fails.

Combined chain in this failure. The likely sequence: the junction runs near or above 125 °C on a hot day, switching loss and leakage rise, a dv/dt transient or Miller current turns on the off device, the leg shoots through, and with no fast short-circuit protection both switches fail short.

Recommended fixes, in order of value: (1) re-rate the heat sink for the worst ambient with margin (about 15 °C below T<sub>j,max</sub>); (2) negative gate bias, dead time and desaturation protection in the driver; (3) a snubber sized from I/(dv/dt), with a non-inductive resistor rated for ½ C<sub>s</sub> V² f<sub>s</sub>; (4) a temperature sensor on the heat sink that derates the current.

Check: the design point satisfies T<sub>j</sub> = 40 + 40 × (1.0 + 0.5 + 0.6) = 124 °C ≤ 125 °C, so the original design was legal but had no margin; the field failure is consistent with operation above the design ambient.

glossary.def: Branch of electronics that converts and controls electric power using semiconductor switches operating as ON/OFF devices.
Two-terminal P-N junction device built with a thick, lightly doped drift layer so it can block high reverse voltage and carry large forward current.
Delay in turning off a diode because stored minority carriers must be removed before it blocks reverse voltage.
Abrupt end of reverse recovery, which produces a sharp current fall and a large voltage spike; a soft recovery avoids it.
Metal–semiconductor diode with no minority carriers, very fast switching and a low forward drop, but limited reverse voltage.
Four-layer P-N-P-N device that turns on when a gate pulse starts internal regeneration and then stays on until anode current falls below holding current.
The three terminals of an SCR: anode and cathode carry the main current, gate receives the control pulse.
Fraction of emitter current that reaches the collector in a transistor; in the two-transistor model, regeneration needs α₁ + α₂ ≥ 1.
Minimum time the SCR needs, after current zero, with reverse voltage applied, before it can block forward voltage again.
Network of L, C and auxiliary switches that forces the anode current of an SCR to zero in a DC circuit.
Load or self-commutation in which a resonant load current itself creates the zero crossing.
AC power control method in which the firing angle of a thyristor or TRIAC sets the portion of each half cycle delivered to the load.
The four combinations of MT2 and gate polarity (measured from MT1) in which a TRIAC can be triggered: I+, I−, III− and III+; sensitivity is poorest in III+.
The largest anode current a GTO can turn off with its gate; above it, gate turn-off fails.
Graph of permitted device current against voltage for a stated pulse width, inside which the device will not be damaged.
Circuit that converts a control signal into the current or voltage pulse a device gate needs, usually with isolation.
Maximum rate of rise of off-state voltage a device can withstand without turning on by itself.
Maximum rate of rise of on-state current allowed at turn-on, set by how fast the conduction area can spread.
Flat part of the gate voltage during switching, while the gate charge swings the drain voltage through C<sub>gd</sub> instead of raising v<sub>GS</sub>.
Temperature of the semiconductor chip itself; it must stay below the rated maximum, typically 125 °C to 175 °C.
Metal structure that carries heat from the device case to the surrounding air, characterised by its thermal resistance in °C/W.
Material such as silicon carbide or gallium nitride with a band gap well above silicon's 1.1 eV, giving a higher breakdown field.
Field strength at which avalanche breakdown begins; about 0.3 MV/cm in silicon and about seven to ten times higher in SiC and GaN.
